traditions.name: Sumerian
traditions.geographic_origin: Southern Mesopotamia (Sumer: Ur, Uruk, Nippur, Eridu, Lagash)
traditions.scholarly_note: Split from the combined 'mesopotamian' record so that Sumerian-language deities and myths can be distinguished from their later Akkadian/Babylonian reinterpretations.

traditions.name: Elamite
traditions.earliest_attestation: c. 2600 BCE (Awan treaty of Naram-Sin, c. 2250 BCE)
traditions.scholarly_note: Elamite religion is known from royal inscriptions and temple remains; much theology is inferred, and identifications between Humban and Napirisha are debated.

traditions.name: Urartian
traditions.scholarly_note: The Meher Kapisi inscription preserves the Urartian state pantheon list with its sacrificial quotas.

traditions.name: Pre-Islamic Arabian (Hejaz / North Arabian)
traditions.earliest_attestation: c. 8th c. BCE (Assyrian records of Arab gods); Hejaz cults to 7th c. CE
traditions.geographic_origin: Arabian Peninsula (Mecca, Ta'if, Nakhla, Qudayd, Dumat al-Jandal)
traditions.scholarly_note: Known mainly through Safaitic, Dadanitic and other North Arabian inscriptions, Herodotus, and the later Islamic Kitab al-Asnam of Hisham ibn al-Kalbi; the Islamic sources are polemical and retrospective.

traditions.name: Nabataean
traditions.scholarly_note: Nabataean religion favoured aniconic standing stones (betyls); Greek writers equated Dushara with Dionysus and later Zeus.

traditions.name: Ancient South Arabian (Sabaean / Minaean / Qatabanian / Hadramite)
traditions.scholarly_note: Each kingdom had a national god (Almaqah of Saba, Wadd of Ma'in, Amm of Qataban, Sayin of Hadramawt) under the shared high god Athtar.

traditions.name: Ammonite / Moabite (Iron Age Transjordan)
traditions.geographic_origin: Moab and Ammon, east of the Jordan
traditions.scholarly_note: Primary evidence is the Mesha Stele and Hebrew Bible polemic; national gods were structurally parallel to Yahweh of Israel.

traditions.name: Aramaean / Syrian (Hierapolis, Palmyra, Damascus)
traditions.scholarly_note: Includes the Syrian Goddess of Hierapolis described by Lucian and the Palmyrene pantheon known from bilingual inscriptions.

traditions.name: Thracian
traditions.geographic_origin: Thrace (modern Bulgaria, northern Greece, European Turkey)
traditions.scholarly_note: Thracian religion is known almost entirely through Greek authors and Roman-era votive reliefs; native theology is reconstructed.

traditions.name: Illyrian
traditions.scholarly_note: Only a handful of Illyrian deity names survive, mostly in Latin dedications; attributions beyond the inscriptions are speculative.

traditions.name: Lusitanian / Hispano-Celtic
traditions.earliest_attestation: Roman-era inscriptions (1st c. BCE–3rd c. CE); Cabeço das Fráguas inscription
traditions.scholarly_note: Deities are known from several hundred Latin and Lusitanian-language votive inscriptions; myths are not preserved.

traditions.name: Ossetian (Nart epic and folk religion)
traditions.earliest_attestation: Nart sagas collected 19th c.; Alanic roots c. 1st millennium CE
traditions.scholarly_note: Ossetians descend from the Iranian-speaking Alans; their Nart epic and dzuar (shrine-spirit) cult blend Iranian, Caucasian and Christian elements.

traditions.name: Circassian / Adyghe (Habze)
traditions.earliest_attestation: Nart epic collected 19th c.; older oral tradition
traditions.scholarly_note: Adyghe Habze is the traditional ethical-religious code; deities are known from Nart tales, prayers and 19th-century ethnography.

traditions.name: Albanian folk religion
traditions.earliest_attestation: Folk tradition recorded 19th–20th c.; some names in medieval/early modern texts
traditions.scholarly_note: Albanian pre-Christian deities survive mainly as folklore beings and calendar names; reconstructions of a pantheon are tentative.

traditions.name: Romano-British / Brittonic
traditions.earliest_attestation: 1st–4th c. CE (Latin inscriptions and curse tablets)
traditions.scholarly_note: Native British deities are known through Latin dedications, often paired with a Roman god (Sulis Minerva, Mars Nodens).

deities.etymology: Sumerian; Suen is the older form that became Akkadian Sîn
deities.summary: The Moon god of Ur, firstborn of Enlil and Ninlil, conceived in the netherworld and raised to the sky. He sails the heavens in his crescent boat, measures the months, and brings the herds and the rising waters. His daughter Inanna and son Utu are the Evening Star and the Sun; his high priestess at Ur was Enheduanna.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2500 BCE (Early Dynastic king list as antediluvian king)
deities.summary: The shepherd who became Inanna's bridegroom and king. When Inanna returned from the Great Below she gave him to the demons as her substitute; his sister Geshtinanna shares his fate so that each spends half the year below. The land mourns him in the dry season and rejoices at his return.

Lady Wind, wife of Enlil and queen of Nippur. Pursued by Enlil and following him into exile below, she bore Nanna and three underworld gods; she sits beside him in the Ekur deciding the fates of the land.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2400 BCE (Gudea of Lagash's personal god)
iconography: entwined serpents on staff (Gudea libation vase)
deities.summary: Serpent-lord of the underworld and personal god of Gudea of Lagash. With Dumuzi he guards the gate of heaven, and below he is throne-bearer of the netherworld and keeper of the roots of trees.
The primeval sea, 'the mother who gave birth to heaven and earth' and to all the gods. At her urging Enki shaped humankind from the clay above the Abzu so that the gods could rest.
The Moon god of Ur and Harran, wise lord who determines the months and reveals omens. Nabonidus raised him above all gods; at Harran his cult endured into the Islamic era.

Tiamat's consort and general, to whom she gave the Tablet of Destinies. After Marduk's victory Kingu was judged guilty of the rebellion and slain; from his blood Ea fashioned humankind to bear the toil of the gods.

primary_sources: Puduhepa's prayer to the Sun Goddess of Arinna/Hebat
iconography: standing on a lion or panther
deities.summary: The Hurrian Queen of Heaven, consort of Teshub, standing on a lion at the head of the goddesses at Yazılıkaya. Queen Puduhepa declared her one with the Sun Goddess of Arinna.

The Storm God of Hatti, king of heaven and husband of the Sun Goddess of Arinna. He drives a chariot drawn by the bulls Sherri and Hurri, wields the thunderbolt, defeats the serpent Illuyanka, and guarantees the treaties of the Hittite kings.

alternate_names: Queen of the Land of Hatti
deities.summary: The supreme goddess of the Hittite state, Queen of Hatti, wife of the Storm God and mother of the weather gods of Nerik and Zippalanda. The Hittite king and queen are her priests; she gives them the kingship.

The farming god, son of the Storm God, who in anger put his shoes on the wrong feet and vanished. With him fertility left the land: the hearth went cold, ewes rejected their lambs, grain did not grow, and the gods starved. A bee sent by Hannahanna stung him awake, and Kamrusepa's rites calmed his rage so that he came home.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1400 BCE (Hurrian Kumarbi cycle in Hittite translation)
primary_sources: Song of Kumarbi / Kingship in Heaven (CTH 344)
deities.summary: The first king in heaven, who ruled nine years until his cupbearer Anu overthrew him and he fled down to the dark earth. His descendant Kumarbi later avenged him on Anu.

The diorite giant begotten by Kumarbi on a great rock to overthrow Teshub. Set on the shoulder of Upelluri, who carries heaven and earth, he grew from the sea until he reached the sky; Ea cut him from his base with the ancient copper knife that once separated heaven from earth.

The serpent who defeated the Storm God. In one telling the goddess Inara feasted him until he could not return to his hole and the mortal Hupasiya bound him; in another he took the Storm God's heart and eyes until the god's son recovered them. Told at the spring purulli festival.

Sister of Teshub, goddess of love, war and healing magic, standing among both the gods and the goddesses at Yazılıkaya. She tried to seduce Ullikummi with music and beauty, and was patron of Hattusili III.
Ruler of the netherworld, to whom the Hittite kings made offerings for health and long life; associated with the Sun Goddess of the Earth who opens the gates of the dead.

primary_sources: Chogha Zanbil temple inscriptions of Untash-Napirisha
deities.summary: Lord of Susa and judge of the dead. He receives souls in the netherworld and weighs their deeds with his assistants Ishmekarab and Lagamal; on earth he is protector of the city and of oaths.
The great god of Elam, lord of heaven and protector of the king, whose name forms the throne names of many Elamite rulers. With Kiririsha and Inshushinak he heads the pantheon.
The Great Goddess of Elam, 'mother of the gods', worshipped at Liyan on the Gulf coast and in the sacred precinct of Chogha Zanbil.

primary_sources: Musasir temple accounts in Sargon II's Eighth Campaign letter
deities.summary: The supreme god of Urartu, whose temple at Musasir held the kingdom's treasures. The kings of Urartu marched 'by the might of Haldi' and attributed all their victories to him.
The Urartian storm and war god, second of the state triad, after whom the fortress-city Teishebaini was named.
The Urartian Sun god, third of the state triad, depicted as a winged sun disc held aloft.

deities.etymology: West Semitic ʿṯtrt, feminine of ʿAthtar (the Venus-star god)
deities.summary: The great goddess of Sidon and Tyre, warrior and lover, 'name of Baal'. Kings of Sidon were her priests; sailors carried her across the Mediterranean to Kition, Carthage, Eryx and Pyrgi.

The healing god of Sidon, whose spring-fed temple at Bustan esh-Sheikh drew the sick for centuries. A youth who castrated himself to escape a goddess's desire and was restored to life by her, he became lord of healing.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 9th c. BCE (Zincirli); prominent at Carthage 5th c. BCE
deities.etymology: Possibly 'lord of the incense altar (ḥmn)' or 'lord of Amanus'
deities.summary: The chief god of Carthage, enthroned between sphinxes, consort of Tanit 'Face of Baal'. Vows to him and Tanit were paid at the tophet; in Roman Africa he lived on as Saturn, lord of the harvest.

iconography: smiting god with mace and shield
deities.summary: The archer god of plague and war, gatekeeper of the underworld at Ugarit. Egyptian pharaohs adopted him as a smiting war god; on Cyprus he was hailed as Apollo.
'Skilful and Wise', the craftsman of the gods, whose home is Kaphtor and Memphis. He forged the clubs Yagrush and Ayamur with which Baal defeated Yam, built Baal's palace, and made Aqhat's bow.

The Sun goddess of Ugarit, 'torch of the gods', who travels by day over the earth and by night through the underworld. She helped Anat carry the dead Baal home and found him again, and rebuked Mot at El's command.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2500 BCE (Malik at Ebla); 7th c. BCE (biblical polemic)
deities.etymology: From Semitic mlk 'king', vocalised in the Hebrew Bible with the vowels of boshet 'shame'
deities.summary: A god of the underworld and the royal dead to whom children were 'passed through the fire' in the valley of Hinnom, according to Israelite prophets who condemned the rite.
The national god of Moab. In Mesha's words, Chemosh was angry with his land and let Israel oppress it, then restored it to Moab and drove Israel out before the king.
The national god of the Ammonites at Rabbah, whose name means 'the king'.

deities.etymology: Aramaic ʿAtarʿateh, combining ʿAthtar/Astarte with ʿAttah/Anat
deities.summary: The great goddess of Hierapolis-Bambyke, mother and protectress of the city and of fish and doves. Her temple housed the throne between lions, and her galli priests served her in ecstatic rites.
Lord of Heaven, the high god of the Aramaeans and Phoenicians, who answered King Zakkur and of whom Philo of Byblos says the Phoenicians held the sun to be him.

deities.earliest_attestation: Nabataean inscription at Hegra (1st c. CE); Meccan cult to 630 CE
deities.summary: The great god of the Kaaba at Mecca, an image of red carnelian with a golden right hand, before whom divining arrows were cast to decide marriages, journeys and disputes.

deities.etymology: Arabic al-ilāt, 'the goddess', feminine of al-ilāh
deities.summary: 'The Goddess', worshipped as a square white stone at Ta'if and across North Arabia and Palmyra. One of the three daughters the Meccans named beside Allah.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. BCE (Dedan inscriptions, debated); Nabataean 1st c. BCE
deities.summary: 'The Mightiest', goddess of the sacred acacias at Nakhla near Mecca, most beloved of the Quraysh, associated with the morning star.
Goddess of fate and allotted portion, worshipped as a black stone at Qudayd on the Red Sea road, especially by the Aws and Khazraj of Yathrib.
The god of love and friendship, national god of the Minaeans, and among the Kalb at Dumat al-Jandal worshipped as a giant armed man. The Quran names him first among the gods of Noah's people.

primary_sources: Nabataean inscriptions at Petra and Hegra
Epiphanius, Panarion 51 (Dusares born of the virgin Chaamou)
deities.etymology: Arabic dhū l-sharā, 'he of the Shara (mountains)'
deities.summary: The supreme god of the Nabataeans and of the royal house, worshipped as a black rectangular stone on a golden base at Petra. At Bostra his festival was the 'Actia Dusaria'.

primary_sources: Awwam (Mahram Bilqis) temple inscriptions at Marib
deities.summary: The national god of Saba, lord of the great Awwam temple at Marib, to whom the mukarribs of Saba dedicated the irrigation works and treaties of the realm. The Sabaeans called themselves 'the children of Almaqah'.

deities.etymology: Common Semitic ʿṯtr; masculine counterpart of Astarte
deities.summary: The highest god of the South Arabian pantheons, invoked first in Sabaean inscriptions, the Venus-star and giver of rain. At Ugarit the same god tried to sit on Baal's throne but his feet did not reach the footstool.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th–4th c. BCE (Artaxerxes II inscriptions); Avestan hymn older
primary_sources: Berossus via Clement of Alexandria, Protrepticus 5
iconography: four-horse chariot of wind, rain, cloud, sleet
deities.summary: The Moist, Strong, Immaculate One: the heavenly river that flows from Mount Hukairya to the sea Vourukasha and purifies the seed of men and the wombs of women. Warriors and kings sacrifice to her for victory; Artaxerxes II invoked her beside Ahura Mazda and Mithra.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1380 BCE (Mitanni treaty, as Mitra); Avesta
deities.etymology: Indo-Iranian *mitra- 'contract, covenant'; cognate of Vedic Mitra
deities.summary: The yazata of the covenant, lord of wide pastures with a thousand ears and ten thousand eyes, who rises before the sun over Mount Hara and smites the contract-breaker with his mace. He is judge of souls with Sraosha and Rashnu at the Chinvat Bridge.
Best Truth, the Amesha Spenta who embodies cosmic order and presides over fire. Through Asha the sun keeps its path and the righteous act rightly; the lie (druj) is his enemy.
Holy Devotion, the Amesha Spenta who is the Earth and the daughter of Ahura Mazda; she rejoices when the earth is farmed and suffers when corpses are buried in her.
Desirable Dominion, the Amesha Spenta of righteous rule and of metals; the kingdom of Ahura Mazda that the faithful long for.
Wholeness and Immortality, the paired Amesha Spentas of waters and plants, who will be the food and drink of the blessed at the renovation of the world.

primary_sources: Nemrut Dağ inscription of Antiochus I (Artagnes-Herakles-Ares)
deities.etymology: Avestan vərəθraγna 'smiting of resistance'; cognate of Vedic vṛtrahan, Indra's epithet 'slayer of Vritra'
deities.summary: The yazata of victory who comes in ten forms — wind, bull, horse, camel, boar, youth, raven, ram, buck, and warrior with a golden blade — to give strength and triumph to the righteous.

The three-headed, six-eyed dragon created by Angra Mainyu to destroy the world of the living. Thraetaona (Fereydun) overcame him and bound him in Mount Damavand, where he waits to break free at the end of time.

The radiant king of the golden age, under whom there was neither heat nor cold, old age nor death. He enlarged the earth three times and built the var, a walled enclosure, to preserve the best of creatures from the great winter; he lost his royal glory through a lie.

The first human, shining like the sun, created by Ahura Mazda. Slain by Angra Mainyu's assault, his seed passed into the earth, and from it grew the rhubarb plant that became Mashya and Mashyana, the first couple.

alternate_names: King of the Paradise of Light
primary_sources: Theodore bar Konai, Liber Scholiorum XI
deities.summary: The God of the Realm of Light, dwelling with his five Shekhinas — Reason, Mind, Intelligence, Thought, Understanding — and his twelve aeons. He does not fight; when Darkness attacked he called forth emanations to go out in his stead.
deities.tradition_claim: The Manichaean scheme of two eternal principles, Light and Darkness

primary_sources: Theodore bar Konai, Liber Scholiorum XI
deities.summary: Lord of the Realm of Darkness, a composite monster with lion head, eagle wings, fish body and dragon feet, ruling five worlds of smoke, fire, wind, water and darkness. Desiring the Light he saw at the border, he invaded it and swallowed the Primal Man's sons, mixing light with matter.

The second emanation, who rescued the Primal Man from the abyss by calling to him, then built the cosmos from the flayed and slain archons: the heavens from their skins, the mountains from their bones, the earth from their flesh.

The emanation who set the sun and moon in motion as ships of light and appeared to the archons in beautiful male and female forms, so that in their lust they released the light they held; from what fell came plants and animals.

alternate_names: Ra-Horakhty who rejoices in the horizon in his name Shu who is in the Aten
deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1900 BCE (as solar disc); exclusive cult under Akhenaten c. 1350 BCE
primary_sources: Great Hymn to the Aten (tomb of Ay, Amarna)
Middle Kingdom Story of Sinuhe (Aten as sun disc)
iconography: solar disc with rays ending in hands
deities.summary: The living sun disc, sole god of Akhenaten's revelation. His rays end in hands that hold the ankh to the nostrils of the king and queen; he alone made the earth according to his desire, and every land and creature lives when he rises.

alternate_names: Father of the Gods (as primeval water)
iconography: bearded man raising the solar barque
deities.summary: The limitless dark water that existed before creation and still surrounds the ordered world. From Nun rose the primeval mound on which Atum came into being; the sun is reborn from him each dawn.
The goddess of Sais, archer and weaver, who at Esna rose from the primeval waters, created the world by speaking seven words, and bore Ra. She is called father of fathers and mother of mothers.
The air and light between heaven and earth, first son of Atum, sneezed or spat out with his sister Tefnut. He holds his daughter Nut aloft above Geb and gives breath to every living thing.
Moisture, daughter of Atum and twin of Shu, mother of Geb and Nut. As the Eye of Ra she once withdrew in anger to Nubia and had to be coaxed home by Thoth and Shu, bringing back the inundation.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2000 BCE (Middle Kingdom apotropaia); popular to Roman period
iconography: frontal dwarf with lion mane and tongue out
deities.summary: The dwarf lion-faced protector of households, mothers and newborns, who dances, plays the tambourine and sticks out his tongue to frighten snakes and demons away.

iconography: black bull with white triangle on brow
deities.summary: The living sacred bull of Memphis, herald and soul of Ptah, recognised by his markings. At death he became Osiris-Apis and was buried in the Serapeum; from him the Ptolemies shaped Serapis.

primary_sources: Book of the Dead, Spell 125 (Papyrus of Ani, Papyrus of Hunefer)
deities.summary: The Devourer who waits beside the scales in the Hall of Two Truths. If a heart is heavier than the feather of Ma'at, she eats it and the soul dies a second death.

deities.etymology: Greek khaos 'gap, chasm', from khainō 'to gape'
deities.summary: First of all things came to be the Chasm. From Chaos were born Erebus and black Night, and from Night Aether and Day.
Primordial Darkness, born from Chaos with Night. By Night he fathered Aether and Day; his name also marks the dark region through which the dead pass to Hades.
The misty pit as far below Hades as heaven is above the earth, walled in bronze, where the Titans are imprisoned. As a primordial god he fathered Typhon on Gaia.
The Titaness of divine law and right order, second wife of Zeus, mother of the Seasons and the Fates; she convenes the assemblies of the gods and once held the oracle at Delphi.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. BCE (Derveni Papyrus refers to Protogonos); Orphic Rhapsodies
deities.etymology: Greek phainō 'to bring to light, shine'
deities.summary: The shining first-born, double-sexed and golden-winged, who burst from the cosmic egg laid by Chronos in the Aether. He revealed all things and was the first king; Zeus later swallowed him and so contained the whole cosmos within himself.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 6th c. BCE (Pherecydes of Syros); Orphic Rhapsodies
deities.summary: Ageless Time, a winged serpent with the heads of a bull, a lion and a god, who with Ananke encircles the cosmos. He produced Aether and Chaos and laid the egg from which Phanes was born.
The queen of the Etruscan gods, consort of Tinia and member of the Capitoline triad with Menrva. At Pyrgi, Thefarie Velianas dedicated a temple to her, which the Phoenician text renders as Astarte.
Goddess of wisdom, war, crafts and health, born armed from Tinia's head and wielder of a thunderbolt; third of the Etruscan triad that passed to the Roman Capitol.
The winged goddess of love and vitality, attended by Lasa spirits; patron of Velch (Vulci).
Messenger of the gods and guide of souls; as Turms Aitas he leads the dead to the underworld.
The winged female underworld spirit who attends the dying and guides the soul on its journey, holding a torch to light the way and a scroll recording the person's fate.
God of wine, vegetation and joyful growth, son of Semla, patron of Pupluna (Populonia).
The youthful armed war god of the Etruscans, lover of Turan.
King of the underworld, enthroned with his queen Phersipnai (Persephone), wearing a wolf-skin cap.

deities.earliest_attestation: Roman-era accounts of Etruscan tradition (Cicero, 1st c. BCE)
primary_sources: Libri Tagetici (lost, cited by Roman authors)
deities.summary: The child-prophet with the wisdom of an old man who rose from a furrow at Tarquinia as the ploughman Tarchon cut it, and dictated the Etrusca disciplina — the art of reading livers and lightning — to the assembled lucumones before vanishing.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. BCE (tradition); attested 3rd c. BCE
deities.etymology: Latin, possibly from favere 'to be favourable'
deities.summary: The horned god of the woods and fields, early king of Latium, who speaks oracles to those who sleep in his groves. The Lupercalia was held in his honour.

deities.earliest_attestation: 296 BCE (temple vowed by Appius Claudius Caecus)
deities.summary: The war goddess of Rome. Before her temple stood the column from which the fetial priest hurled a spear to declare war, and there the Senate received envoys and victorious generals.
Goddess of luck and fate, with her great oracle at Praeneste where children drew the oak lots. She holds the rudder that steers and the cornucopia that gives, and stands on the wheel that turns.
The punisher of broken oaths and god of the dead, who drags the dying away; in folk speech his name lived on as the ogre.

The god of the Getae, to whom every fifth year a messenger was sent by being thrown onto spears. He taught that neither he nor his guests would die but would go to a place where they would live forever; he withdrew into an underground chamber for three years and reappeared.
deities.tradition_claim: Herodotus records the Greek counter-claim that Zalmoxis was a former slave of Pythagoras; the Getae revered him as a god.

deities.summary: The Thracian huntress and moon goddess whose cult Athens admitted at Piraeus; her festival the Bendideia featured a torch race on horseback.

iconography: votive bronze hand in benediction gesture
deities.summary: The horseman and sky-father of the Thracians and Phrygians, worshipped with nocturnal mysteries in which a snake was drawn through the initiate's robe. His votive hands, raised in blessing and covered with symbols, were dedicated across the empire.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 4th c. BCE; thousands of reliefs 2nd–3rd c. CE
primary_sources: Votive reliefs from Bulgaria, Romania and northern Greece
Greek and Latin dedications (Heroi, Deo Heroni)
deities.summary: The divine rider shown galloping toward an altar or tree around which a serpent coils, spearing a boar or other beast. He protects the living, heals, and guides the dead.

primary_sources: CIL VIII 2581 (Lambaesis dedication by a legate from Risinium)
deities.summary: The protector-god of Risinium (Risan, Montenegro), described in a Latin verse dedication as a lofty rider with a lance.

primary_sources: Votive altars from the Privilica spring near Bihać (Iapodes)
deities.summary: God of springs and waters among the Iapodes, honoured with altars at a sacred spring and equated by the Romans with Neptune.

deities.earliest_attestation: Roman era (sanctuary at São Miguel da Mota, Alandroal)
primary_sources: Over 80 votive inscriptions from São Miguel da Mota (Portugal)
deities.summary: The god of the hill-sanctuary of São Miguel da Mota, invoked for health and protection and consulted through incubation; worship of him continued among Romanised Lusitanians as 'most present and powerful god'.

primary_sources: Votive inscriptions from Turobriga and Mérida (Emerita Augusta)
deities.summary: The goddess of Turobriga, of rebirth and spring, identified with Proserpina; curse tablets asked her to punish thieves.

primary_sources: Votive inscriptions and paterae from Lusitania and Gallaecia
deities.summary: A protector god of communities and warriors, worshipped under many local epithets as guardian of a settlement or group.
Goddess of rivers, springs and valleys in Gallaecia and northern Lusitania, honoured at the Fonte do Ídolo in Braga.
The sky-father of the Scythians, husband of Api the Earth and ancestor of the royal line through Targitaos. Herodotus says the Scythians rightly call Zeus Papaios.
The Earth goddess of the Scythians, wife of Papaios.
The Scythian goddess identified with Heavenly Aphrodite, who gave the gift of divination to the Enarees, her androgynous priests.

primary_sources: Helmold of Bosau, Chronica Slavorum I.52
deities.summary: The Black God of the Baltic Slavs, to whom curses were spoken at feasts as the cup was passed: all misfortune comes from him.

deities.earliest_attestation: Inferred from Helmold (12th c.); name attested only later
primary_sources: Helmold of Bosau, Chronica Slavorum I.52 (implied good god)
deities.summary: The White God, giver of good fortune, the bright counterpart of Chernobog.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 980 CE (Vladimir's pantheon in the Primary Chronicle)
primary_sources: Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let), entry for 980
deities.summary: One of the gods whose idols Vladimir set on the hill at Kiev. The winds are called his grandchildren, blowing arrows from the sea.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th–12th c. CE (Old Russian anti-pagan sermons)
primary_sources: Slovo nekoego khristolyubtsa (Word of a Christ-lover)
deities.summary: The god of kin and birth, to whom bread, cheese and honey were set out with the Rozhanitsy, the birth-fate maidens; he breathes life into the newborn and destines it.

The four-headed god of Arkona on Rügen, holding a horn of wine from which the priest read the coming year's harvest, and owning a white horse whose steps through rows of spears foretold war. His temple fell to the Danes in 1168.

deities.earliest_attestation: 16th c. CE (Jan Łasicki, De diis Samagitarum)
deities.summary: The Earth goddess who brings forth all life, greeted with a kiss by those who rise in the morning, and given the first drops of beer and bread at every meal. The dead return to her.

deities.earliest_attestation: 16th c. CE (Christian sources as devil); older folk tradition
primary_sources: Lithuanian and Latvian folk tales and dainas
deities.etymology: Baltic *vel- 'dead' (cf. Lithuanian vėlės 'souls of the dead')
deities.summary: Lord of the dead and of the underworld, cunning shape-shifter and owner of wealth, eternally pursued by Perkūnas who strikes him with thunder. Under Christianity he became the devil, often outwitted by a clever peasant.
The Moon, husband of Saulė the Sun. When he fell in love with Aušrinė the Morning Star, Perkūnas cut him in pieces, which is why the moon waxes and wanes; the stars are the children of Sun and Moon.

primary_sources: Karelian creation runes collected by Elias Lönnrot
deities.summary: The virgin daughter of the air who descended to the sea and floated for seven hundred years. A teal laid its eggs on her knee; when they broke, the lower halves became the earth, the upper the sky, the yolk the sun, the white the moon. She shaped the shores and bore Väinämöinen.
Lord of Tuonela, the land of the dead beyond the black river where the swan swims. With his wife Tuonetar and their daughters he keeps the dead; Väinämöinen barely escaped his nets.

primary_sources: Mikael Agricola, preface to the Psalter (1551)
deities.summary: The king of the sea and the waters, with his wife Vellamo. Agricola wrote that Ahti brought fish from the water; fishermen asked his favour.

primary_sources: Mikael Agricola, preface to the Psalter (1551)
deities.summary: The bearded king of the forest, with his wife Mielikki ruling Tapiola. Hunters prayed to him to open his storehouses of game.

The reckless, handsome hero who, sent to shoot the swan of Tuonela, was killed and his body cut to pieces in the river of the dead. His mother raked his pieces from the water with a copper rake, joined them, and a bee brought balm from heaven to restore him to life.

deities.earliest_attestation: Folk runes; 1551 CE (Agricola: Ilmarinen gives calm and storm)
primary_sources: Mikael Agricola, preface to the Psalter (1551)
deities.summary: The eternal smith who hammered the vault of the sky so skilfully that no seam shows, and forged the Sampo, the mill of plenty, as the bride-price for the Maiden of Pohjola.

primary_sources: Mikael Agricola, preface to the Psalter (1551)
deities.summary: Once the sacred grove where the dead were honoured, Hiisi became a forest demon and giant who sends sickness and evil; his elk is chased by Lemminkäinen.

deities.etymology: From Norse Þórr karl, 'Old Man Thor'
iconography: wooden image with nail and flint in the head
deities.summary: The thunder god who drives away trolls and evil spirits with his two hammers, and who also governs rain and the sea. His wooden image was raised with hammers at sacred sites.
The ruling father, highest of the gods, who is mostly at rest and acts through his son Rádienbárdni. He gives souls to Máttaráhkká to be carried into the world.
Daughter of Máttaráhkká who receives the child's body into the mother and helps women in labour; she lived under the hearth, and porridge was offered to her after a birth.
Daughter of Máttaráhkká who can turn an unborn girl into a boy and who watches over children and hunters; a small bow was set in the porridge in her honour.
Daughter of Máttaráhkká who lives under the threshold of the goahti, guarding those who go in and out and the newborn in its first steps.
The old woman who rules Jábmiidáibmu, the realm of the dead beneath the earth. Black animals were buried alive to her to ransom the sick.
The great god of the Oeselians, born, they said, on a wooded hill in Vironia and flown from there to Saaremaa; his grove was felled by the crusaders.

primary_sources: Estonian folk tales (Kaval-Ants and Vanapagan cycle)
Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald, Eesti rahva ennemuistsed jutud (1866)
deities.summary: The Old Heathen, a giant farmer of the other world, strong and dim, forever cheated by his clever farmhand Kaval-Ants. The church made him the devil.

deities.earliest_attestation: Medieval Hungarian texts; folk legends recorded 19th–20th c.
deities.summary: In Hungarian folk creation tales, Isten sends Ördög down to the bottom of the primeval sea to bring up sand; Ördög hides some in his mouth, and it swells into the mountains. He is Isten's companion-adversary in the making of the world.
deities.tradition_claim: The dualist earth-diver legend is shared across Eastern European folk Christianity.

primary_sources: Basque legends collected by José Miguel de Barandiarán
deities.summary: The hairy giant lord of the woods who guards the flocks, warns shepherds of storms with his cry, and once held the secrets of sowing grain and forging, until San Martin Txiki tricked them from him.

primary_sources: Basque folk prayers and customs collected by José Miguel de Barandiarán
deities.summary: Grandmother Sun, daughter of Ama Lurra (Mother Earth), to whom she returns each night. She was created to drive away the night spirits, and the eguzkilore (sun-thistle) on doors stands for her.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 3rd c. BCE (by chronicle tradition, King Pharnavaz); recorded in medieval chronicles
primary_sources: Life of St Nino (Conversion of Kartli)
deities.etymology: Often derived from Ahura Mazda (via Armenian Aramazd), though a local origin is also proposed
deities.summary: The chief idol and god of Kartli, set up by King Pharnavaz on the mountain above Mtskheta: a man of copper in golden armour with emerald and beryl eyes and a turning sword. St Nino's prayer brought down hail that shattered him.

deities.earliest_attestation: Nart sagas and dzuar cult, recorded 19th c.
deities.summary: The protector of men, warriors and travellers, the most honoured of the dzuars. Riding a white horse with three legs he appears among the Narts; women may not speak his name.

The greatest Nart hero, born from a swelling on his father's back and tempered steel-hard in the forge of Kurdalægon. He fought the heavenly spirits themselves; dying, he demanded his sword be thrown into the sea, and when it was, the sea turned blood-red and boiled.
Lord of thunder and of the wheat, who protects the harvest and strikes with lightning. Those killed by lightning are his, buried where they fell, and a ram is sacrificed to him.

primary_sources: Ossetian Nart sagas (Soslan in the Land of the Dead)
deities.summary: Ruler of the land of the dead, who decides where each soul will go, to paradise or hell, and receives the dead at the gate of his realm.
The smith of heaven who forges weapons for the Narts, mends Batradz's body and tempers him in his forge, and gives iron lips to the dead.
The one great god of the Adyghe, creator of all, above the other powers; prayers begin and end with his name.
The god of thunder and lightning; a person or animal struck by lightning was considered chosen and was honoured with dances and songs.
The smith of the Narts and god of the forge, who made the first iron tools and weapons, forged the sickle for the harvest, and sought the end of the world.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. CE recording (Movses Khorenatsi, Agathangelos) of older tradition
primary_sources: Movses Khorenatsi, History of Armenia I.31
Agathangelos, History of the Armenians (temple of Ashtishat)
deities.etymology: Middle Iranian Varhagn, from Avestan Verethragna
deities.summary: The fiery god born when heaven, earth and the purple sea were in labour: from a reed came smoke, then flame, and from the flame a youth with hair and beard of fire and eyes like suns. He fought and reaped the dragons and stole straw from Barsham, scattering it across the sky as the Milky Way.
Goddess of love, beauty and water, beloved of Vahagn, worshipped with him at Ashtishat. At the summer festival of Vardavar people splash one another with water in her honour.

primary_sources: Agathangelos, History of the Armenians (temple of Tir near Artashat)
deities.summary: The scribe of Aramazd, god of writing, learning and dream-interpretation, who records the fate of each person; his temple stood near Artashat.

primary_sources: Eznik of Kolb, Against the Sects
deities.summary: The Earth and the underworld below it, realm of the dead; in the Armenian translation of 2 Maccabees her name renders that of Dionysus.
The sky and the god who dwells in it; the word for God in Albanian, which in folk use also names the heavens and the thunder that falls from them.

deities.earliest_attestation: Calendar name (e enjte, Thursday) and folk tradition
deities.summary: The fire god honoured in the hearth, whose day is Thursday; fire is sworn by and never spat into.
A semi-divine winged hero, born with a caul and small wings under his arms, who fights the kulshedra with lightning, thrown boulders and uprooted trees to release the waters.
The many-headed female dragon who withholds the waters, causing drought, or spews fire and floods; she grows from the bolla serpent that has gone unseen for years. The drangue is her eternal foe.

The god of the Gauls whom Caesar called Mercury, inventor of all the arts, guide on roads and journeys, and the greatest power over trade. Lugdunum, 'fort of Lugus', was his city, and the assembly of the Gauls met there in August.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 60 CE (Lucan); Pillar of the Boatmen (14–37 CE)
deities.summary: One of the three gods to whom Lucan says the Gauls gave cruel offerings. On the Pillar of the Boatmen he hews a tree in which a bull and three cranes stand; the Berne scholiast says his victims were hung from trees.
The bright healing god, patron of Aquileia and Noricum, whose priests served him at Bayeux; the Romans called him Apollo.

The Gauls' Herakles: an old man, bald and sun-browned, with club and bow, who leads a crowd of men by thin chains of gold and amber running from his tongue to their ears — eloquence that binds stronger than force.

primary_sources: Gallo-Roman dedications pairing her with Mercury
Gloucester relief of Mercury and Rosmerta
deities.summary: The Great Provider, goddess of abundance, paired with Mercury across Gaul and the Rhineland.

primary_sources: Math fab Mathonwy (Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi)
deities.summary: Son of Arianrhod, who laid three curses on him — no name, no arms, no human wife — which Gwydion broke by trickery. Struck by Gronw's spear in a posture neither indoors nor out, he flew up as an eagle, rotting in an oak, until Gwydion sang him down and restored him.

primary_sources: Branwen ferch Llŷr (Second Branch of the Mabinogi)
deities.summary: The giant king of the Island of the Mighty who waded the sea to Ireland and lay as a bridge for his army. Wounded by a poisoned spear, he bade his men cut off his head, which spoke and feasted with them for eighty years and was buried at the White Mount in London to guard Britain from invasion.

deities.earliest_attestation: Culhwch and Olwen (c. 1100); Maponos inscriptions 2nd–3rd c. CE
primary_sources: Romano-British inscriptions to (Apollo) Maponus at Hadrian's Wall (RIB)
deities.summary: The Great Son of the Great Mother, stolen from his mother when three nights old and imprisoned in Caer Loyw until Arthur's men, guided by the oldest animals, freed him to hunt the boar Twrch Trwyth.

deities.earliest_attestation: Culhwch and Olwen; Welsh Triads; Matrona inscriptions
deities.summary: The Great Mother, mother of Mabon, remembered in the Triads as the mother of Owain and Morfudd by Urien.
The goddess of the hot springs at Bath, where an undying fire burned on her altar. Those wronged threw lead curse tablets into her spring, asking her to punish thieves.

deities.etymology: Celtic *noudont- 'catcher, acquirer'; cognate of Irish Nuadu
deities.summary: God of the great healing sanctuary at Lydney above the Severn, with its dormitory for incubation and votive dogs; one man cursed the thief of his ring in his name.
The Sun, invoked in the Merseburg charm with her sister Sinthgunt to heal the foal of Balder; in Norse tradition she drives the sun's chariot chased by the wolf Sköll.
The goddess of the Marsi whose much-frequented temple Germanicus razed during an autumn festival.
The Frisian goddess whose sacred grove was the place where nine hundred Roman soldiers were cut down during the revolt of 28 CE.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Moon and the Months
facets.core_claim: Nanna is the radiant crescent who orders the months; at his new-moon rising the cattle multiply and the land is fed.

facets.facet_name: Father of the Sun and the Evening Star
facets.core_claim: From Nanna come Utu the Sun and Inanna the Evening Star: the lights of heaven descend from the Moon.

facets.facet_name: The Bridegroom Taken to the Netherworld
facets.core_claim: Dumuzi goes down to the land of no return in Inanna's place and comes up again for half the year; his descent is the withering of the pasture and his return its greening.
As Inanna's chosen husband Dumuzi is the model of the king who weds the goddess so that the land prospers.
Ninlil shares Enlil's throne and with him decrees destinies; her children are the Moon and the lords of the underworld.

facets.facet_name: Serpent Gatekeeper Between Heaven and the Netherworld
facets.core_claim: Ningishzida coils between the realms: he stands at Anu's gate with Dumuzi, and below he keeps the roots and the throne of the dead.

facets.facet_name: The Mother Who Bore Heaven and Earth
facets.core_claim: Before An and Ki were separated there was Nammu, the waters without beginning, and from her all gods were born.
Nammu wakes Enki from sleep and sets him to fashion humankind from the clay of the Abzu.

facets.facet_name: Champion of Enlil, Slayer of Anzu and Asag
facets.core_claim: Ninurta, son of Enlil, defeats Asag and the stone warriors of the mountains, recovers the Tablet of Destinies from Anzu, and turns the conquered stones into dykes that water the fields.
Ishkur rides the storm and brings rain to the uplands or withholds it; he is the roaring lion-dragon of the clouds.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Harran, King of the Gods (Nabonidus)
facets.core_claim: Sîn is lord of the crown of heaven; the gods tremble before him, and the king who honours him is given dominion.

facets.facet_name: Holder of the Tablet of Destinies for Tiamat
facets.core_claim: Kingu was raised by Tiamat to supreme command and wore the Tablet of Destinies that belongs only to the rightful king of the gods.

facets.facet_name: The God Whose Blood Became Humanity
facets.core_claim: Humankind is made from the blood of the slain rebel god, so that people carry divine substance and the burden of service.

facets.facet_name: Queen of Heaven, Consort of the Storm King
facets.core_claim: Hebat leads the procession of goddesses to meet Teshub; she is mother of Sharruma and queen of all the gods.

facets.facet_name: Storm God of Hatti, King of Heaven
facets.core_claim: Tarhunz is the conqueror: he thunders from the mountains, brings rain to the fields, and the Great King rules Hatti as his steward.

facets.facet_name: Sun Goddess, Queen of the Land of Hatti
facets.core_claim: The Sun Goddess of Arinna holds the kingship of Hatti and entrusts it to the Great King; she is the light that judges and protects the land.

facets.facet_name: The God Who Vanished and Returned
facets.core_claim: When Telipinu turns away in anger, all growth stops in heaven and earth; when he is found and soothed, abundance returns and the eya-tree is hung with plenty.
Alalu sat on the throne of heaven in the earliest days; Anu, who bowed at his feet, deposed him and he went below.

facets.facet_name: The Stone Giant Who Rose Against Heaven
facets.core_claim: Ullikummi, deaf and blind stone, grows to threaten the gods' city until his feet are severed from the bearer of the world.

facets.facet_name: The Serpent Who Overcame the Storm God
facets.core_claim: Illuyanka once beat the Storm God and held his strength, until he was tricked, bound and slain so that the land could flourish.

facets.facet_name: Hurrian Goddess of Love and War
facets.core_claim: Shaushka moves between battle and desire, between the gods and the goddesses; she charms monsters and grants victory to her favourites.
Lelwani keeps the dark earth where the dead go down; the king's life may be ransomed by gifts to her house.

facets.facet_name: Judge of the Dead at Susa
facets.core_claim: Inshushinak sits in judgment over the souls brought before him and assigns each its fate in the world below.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Susa and Guardian of Oaths
facets.core_claim: The kings of Elam rule as servants of Inshushinak, lord of Susa, and swear by his name.
Humban is the great one who extends his protection over the king and the land of Elam.
facets.scholarly_note: Whether Napirisha ('great god') is an epithet of Humban or a separate deity is debated; this record follows the identification only as a possibility.

facets.facet_name: Great Goddess and Mother of the Gods
facets.core_claim: Kiririsha is the great lady and mother of the gods, worshipped beside the great god in his ziggurat.
Haldi goes before the army; through him the king conquers, and to him the first share of every victory is given.

facets.facet_name: Storm and War God of Urartu
facets.core_claim: Teisheba thunders over the highlands and fights beside Haldi for the king of Urartu.
Shivini is the sun that sees all the land, third of the great gods of Urartu.
Astarte is the bright goddess of desire and of the hunt and battle; Sidon is her city and its kings her priests.
Astarte is the planet that rises at dusk, the heavenly lady of the West Semitic world.
Eshmun heals at the sacred spring; the sick bathe in his waters and give thanks with images of the children he restored.
Eshmun died young and was made divine by the goddess who loved him.
facets.scholarly_note: The castration-and-revival story is known only from the late Neoplatonist Damascius.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Carthage and the Harvest
facets.core_claim: Baal Hammon is the old king of the gods of Carthage, who gives the harvest and receives the vows of the city.
facets.scholarly_note: The meaning of the tophet offerings (child sacrifice versus burial of infants) remains debated.

facets.core_claim: Resheph shoots arrows of pestilence and stands guard at the gate of the dead; yet he who sends the plague can also turn it away.
Kothar forges the weapons of victory and raises the house of the king of the gods; his skill is a kind of wisdom and spell.

facets.facet_name: Torch of the Gods Who Passes Through the Underworld
facets.core_claim: Shapash crosses into the land of the dead each night; she carries the fallen and brings word between the living gods and those below.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Offering Through Fire
facets.core_claim: To Molek, king of the dead, the firstborn were given at the Tophet; the prophets of Yahweh named this the greatest abomination.
facets.scholarly_note: Since Otto Eissfeldt (1935) many scholars read molk as a sacrifice term rather than a god's name; others accept a deity Malik/Milku. Biblical sources are hostile.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Grain and Father of Baal
facets.core_claim: Dagan is the grain-lord of the Middle Euphrates and of the Philistine coast, father of Baal and giver of the harvest.
facets.scholarly_note: The medieval derivation of the name from Hebrew dag 'fish' is folk etymology; Dagan is a grain god (Ugaritic dgn 'grain').

facets.core_claim: Chemosh is lord of Moab: his anger brings defeat, his favour brings victory, and captured cities are devoted to him.
Milcom is the king of the Ammonites who wears the great crown of Rabbah.
Atargatis sits enthroned between lions as mother of the city; her sacred fish and doves are never harmed.
Baalshamin is master of the heavens, who gives rain and answers kings who lift their hands to him.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Kaaba's Divining Arrows
facets.core_claim: Hubal stood within the House at Mecca; the Quraysh cast the arrows before him, and his answer settled what they should do.
Allat is the goddess, guardian of her sanctuary and of those who take refuge there; her stone at Ta'if was clothed and honoured.
With al-Uzza and Manat she was called upon as an intercessor whose favour is hoped for.
facets.scholarly_note: The Quran (53:19–23) rejects the claim that these are daughters of God.

facets.facet_name: The Mightiest, Goddess of the Morning Star
facets.core_claim: Al-Uzza, the Mighty, dwells in the three acacias of Nakhla; the Quraysh made their circuit for her and called her in battle.
Manat measures each person's share and the hour of their death; pilgrims shaved their heads at her shrine.
Wadd is love and amity; 'Wadd is father' said the Minaeans, and they placed their land under his protection.
facets.scholarly_note: Wadd's lunar character is often asserted but rests on the serpent-and-crescent iconography; it is not certain.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Mountains, God of the King
facets.core_claim: Dushara is lord of the Shara; his throne is the stone, and the Nabataean kings ruled as his people.
Almaqah is lord of Saba; the dam and the fields are his, and the people of Saba are his children.

facets.facet_name: The Morning Star, First of the Gods
facets.core_claim: ʿAthtar is invoked first of the gods; he waters the fields and his star rises in the east.

facets.facet_name: The Star Who Could Not Fill Baal's Throne
facets.core_claim: When Baal died, ʿAthtar the Terrible was set on the throne of Zaphon; his feet did not reach the stool, and he came down to rule the earth.
Aredvi Sura Anahita pours down from the heights as all the waters of the world, cleansing seed and womb and giving milk to mothers.
Heroes from Yima to Vishtaspa offered to Anahita, and she gave them victory over their enemies.
Mithra is the contract itself: he watches every agreement and destroys the house and lands of the Mithra-deceiver.

facets.facet_name: Herald of the Sun and Judge of Souls
facets.core_claim: Mithra rides out before the immortal swift-horsed Sun and stands at the Bridge where souls are judged.

facets.facet_name: Good Mind, First of the Amesha Spentas
facets.core_claim: Vohu Manah, the Good Mind, is the first creation of Ahura Mazda; he welcomed Zarathustra to the presence of the Wise Lord and receives the righteous soul in paradise. Cattle are his creation.
Asha Vahishta is the order of the world made holy; every fire tended and every truth spoken is his.
Spenta Armaiti is the earth and humble devotion together; she bears all creatures and is gladdened by the ploughman.
Khshathra Vairya is the rule of the good that will come in fullness; metal and the strength to protect the poor are his.
Haurvatat gives health and the waters; Ameretat gives deathlessness and the plants; together they are the reward of the righteous.

facets.facet_name: Smiter of Resistance, Giver of Victory
facets.core_claim: Verethragna, best-armed of the yazatas, breaks the resistance of enemies and comes to the faithful in ten forms.

facets.facet_name: The Three-Headed Dragon of the Lie
facets.core_claim: Azhi Dahaka, full of a thousand sorceries, was made by the Evil Spirit to empty the world of the righteous; bound under Damavand, he will be loosed and slain at the renovation.

facets.facet_name: King of the Golden Age and the Var
facets.core_claim: Yima ruled a thousand years without death; when the winters came he built the var and sheltered the seed of every good creature.

facets.facet_name: The Primal Man Whose Death Seeded Humanity
facets.core_claim: Gayomart died at the onset of evil, and from his body the metals and from his seed humankind came forth.

facets.facet_name: King of the Realm of Light
facets.core_claim: The Father of Greatness is light without limit, the one root of all good; nothing evil can touch his kingdom.

facets.facet_name: The Ruler of Darkness Who Invaded the Light
facets.core_claim: The Prince of Darkness is eternal evil and desire; he rose against the Light, devoured its particles, and binds them in matter until the end.

facets.facet_name: Builder of the Cosmos from the Bodies of Archons
facets.core_claim: The Living Spirit fashions the world as a great machine for refining the captive light back to its source.

facets.facet_name: Pilot of the Ships of Light
facets.core_claim: The Messenger shows his beauty to the powers of darkness and draws the stolen light up through the moon and sun to the Father.

facets.facet_name: The Primal Man Who Gave Himself to the Darkness
facets.core_claim: Called forth by the Mother of Life, the Primal Man armed himself with his five sons, the light-elements, and let them be swallowed by Darkness as bait; rescued by the Living Spirit, he left his armour behind as the light scattered in the world.

facets.facet_name: Apostle of Light and Seal of the Prophets
facets.core_claim: Mani, visited by his heavenly Twin, is the last apostle after Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus, who brought the complete revelation of the two principles and the three times.

facets.facet_name: The Sole God, Creator of All
facets.core_claim: O sole god, like whom there is no other! You made the earth as you wished, you alone; when you rise all live, when you set they die.

facets.facet_name: The Disc Whose Rays Give Life
facets.core_claim: The Aten's rays reach down as hands to the king, his only son who knows him, and through the king life passes to the land.
Before heaven and earth, before the gods, there was Nun, inert and boundless; all things came out of him and all are still encircled by him.
Neith emerged from Nun, spoke the world into being in seven words and gave birth to Ra; she is the self-generated mother.
Neith's crossed arrows guard the king and the dead.

facets.facet_name: The Air That Holds Heaven Apart
facets.core_claim: Shu stands between Geb and Nut and lifts the sky; in him all breathe, and he is the life that Atum breathed out.
Tefnut is the dew and the order of moisture; when she departs as the raging lioness, the land dries, and when she returns it is renewed.

facets.facet_name: Guardian of Birth and the Home
facets.core_claim: Bes watches over women in childbirth and over sleeping children; his grimace and his dancing drive off every evil.

facets.facet_name: The Living Bull, Herald of Ptah
facets.core_claim: Apis is Ptah's living image on earth; at his death he goes to Osiris, and a new Apis is born.
Ammit crouches by the balance: the heart that fails the weighing is hers, and its owner ceases to exist.
Atum, the Complete One, came into being by himself on the primeval mound out of Nun and generated Shu and Tefnut from his own substance; at the end of time he alone will remain with Osiris.

facets.facet_name: Protective Cat and Gentle Eye of Ra
facets.core_claim: Bastet of Bubastis guards home and mother; she is the lioness pacified into the cat, the gentle Eye of Ra.
Before Earth, before Eros, there was the yawning gap; all darkness and all light descend from it.
Black Night, born of Chaos, bore Day and Aether, and alone bore Death, Sleep, Dreams, the Fates and Nemesis; even Zeus fears to displease her.
Erebus is the deep darkness that existed from the first and lies beneath the earth on the road of the dead.

facets.facet_name: The Abyss-Prison of the Defeated Gods
facets.core_claim: Tartarus is the bottom of the world: a bronze anvil would fall nine days to reach it, and there the overthrown powers are bound.
Themis is what is fitting by divine ordinance; she sits beside Zeus and calls the gods to assembly.

facets.facet_name: The First Sky, Overthrown by His Son
facets.core_claim: Ouranos covered Gaia and would not let their children be born; Kronos castrated him with the adamant sickle, and from his blood came the Erinyes and from the foam Aphrodite.

facets.facet_name: Primordial Desire That Joins All Things
facets.core_claim: Eros, fairest of the deathless gods, came into being with Earth at the beginning; he loosens limbs and makes all generation possible.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Wild, Flocks and Panic
facets.core_claim: Goat-footed Pan roams the Arcadian heights, piping on the syrinx; he guards shepherds and sends sudden panic on those who intrude.
Thanatos, son of Night, comes to mortals at their hour; iron-hearted, he takes them gently to the house of Hades.

facets.facet_name: The First-Born Who Brings All to Light
facets.core_claim: Phanes leapt from the silver egg and lit up the dark; he holds the seeds of the gods, and from him the world is made manifest.

facets.facet_name: Swallowed by Zeus, Reborn as the Cosmos
facets.core_claim: When Zeus swallowed Phanes, all things were made new within Zeus: the first-born lives on as the inside of the world.

facets.facet_name: Ageless Time, Layer of the Cosmic Egg
facets.core_claim: Before all gods was unaging Chronos, coiled with Necessity around the world; from him came the egg of all things.
facets.scholarly_note: Distinct from the Titan Kronos, though ancient writers often played on the two names.

facets.facet_name: Queen of the Gods, Protectress of the City
facets.core_claim: Uni is the great queen beside Tinia; she gives kingship and suckles the hero who becomes divine.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of Wisdom, War and Crafts
facets.core_claim: Menrva springs armed from the head of Tinia; she counsels heroes and hurls one of the thunderbolts.
Turan is the lady of desire, winged and adorned, who unites lovers and gives life its bloom.
Turms carries the word of the gods and leads souls down to Aita's house.
Vanth is present at the moment of death; she lights the dead one's road with her torch and keeps the record of their fate.
Fufluns is the rising sap and the vine; with him come feast and revel.
Laran is the young warrior in helmet and cuirass, spear in hand.
Aita rules the house of the dead with Phersipnai; the wolf's head is his crown.
Tages sprang from the earth and taught the twelve lords of Etruria how to read the will of the gods; all haruspicy is his gift.

facets.facet_name: Woodland God and Oracle of Dreams
facets.core_claim: Faunus protects the herds and fields and speaks in dreams to those who sleep on the fleeces of sacrifice in his grove.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of War and Its Declaration
facets.core_claim: Bellona drives the chariot of battle; war is not begun until the spear is cast from her column.
Fortuna guides every life with her rudder and pours plenty from her horn; her wheel lifts and casts down.

facets.facet_name: Punisher of Broken Oaths, Taker of the Dead
facets.core_claim: Orcus seizes those whose time has come and punishes the oath-breaker in the world below.
Quirinus is the god of the Roman people in assembly, the Quirites; Romulus was taken up into heaven and revealed himself as Quirinus.
facets.scholarly_note: Dumézil placed Quirinus as the third-function member of the archaic Jupiter–Mars–Quirinus triad; this is contested.

facets.core_claim: Terminus is the stone that marks the field; when Jupiter's temple was built on the Capitol, Terminus alone would not move, and so the boundary of Rome would never retreat.
Saturn, fleeing Jupiter, hid in Latium and taught its people to farm; his reign was the Golden Age, recalled each Saturnalia when masters served slaves.

facets.facet_name: Teacher of Immortality Who Returned from Hiding
facets.core_claim: Zalmoxis promised the Getae that they do not die but go to him; he vanished below the earth and came back in the fourth year.
Bendis hunts with two spears in the forests of Thrace and rides the night with torches.
Sabazios is the lord of heaven who comes to his initiates as a serpent; his raised hand blesses and protects.

facets.facet_name: The Divine Rider at the Serpent Tree
facets.core_claim: Heros rides out from the sacred tree to protect, to heal and to carry the heroised dead.
Medaurus rides high above Risinium with his lance, guarding the city and those who come from it.
Bindus is the spirit of the spring that rises from the rock; the Iapodes' chieftains set their altars at his waters.
Endovelicus answers those who sleep in his sanctuary, healing them and granting what they vow for.
facets.scholarly_note: His chthonic character is inferred from boar iconography and dream-oracle practice.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of Rebirth and Avenging Justice
facets.core_claim: Ataegina brings the spring back from below and avenges wrongs brought to her in writing.
Bandua binds a people together and defends them; each town calls him by its own name.
Nabia lives in the spring and the river valley; to her the waters and the herds that drink them belong.
Papaios is the father of the Scythians; with Earth he begot the first man Targitaos.
Api is the earth and its waters, the mother of the Scythian race.
Argimpasa grants the Enarees their power to prophesy with the linden bark.
Dazhbog is the sun, son of Svarog, the god who gives; the people of Rus' are called his grandchildren.

facets.facet_name: Celestial Smith and Father of the Sun
facets.core_claim: Svarog, whom the chronicler called Hephaestus, forged the first tongs from heaven, established marriage and law, and fathered the sun Dazhbog.

facets.facet_name: Winter and Death, Drowned at Spring
facets.core_claim: Morana is the death of the year: her straw image is carried out of the village, burned or drowned, so that spring may enter.
Chernobog is the evil god; at the feast the cup is passed and his name spoken over it, for all ill fortune is in his power.

facets.facet_name: The White God of Good Fortune
facets.core_claim: Belobog gives all good things, as Chernobog sends the bad; the bright and the black divide the world between them.
facets.scholarly_note: No medieval source names Belobog; he is a modern inference from Helmold's statement that the Slavs believed in a good god opposed to the black god.

facets.core_claim: The winds are Stribog's grandchildren; they rush from the sea and drive arrows into the ranks of warriors.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Kin, Birth and Destiny
facets.core_claim: Rod and the Rozhanitsy stand at every birth and give the child its fate; to them the table is laid at the feast of kin.
facets.scholarly_note: Modern reconstructions making Rod the supreme creator of the Slavs go beyond the sermons, which list him with lesser powers.

facets.core_claim: Svantevit looks to all four quarters; his horn tells the harvest, his horse tells the war, and all the Rani bring him tribute.
Žemyna, the flowerer, feeds all that lives and takes back the dead; she is honoured first at the table.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Dead, Foe of the Thunderer
facets.core_claim: Velnias hides in trees, stones and animals; wherever he hides Perkūnas strikes, and the dead are his flock.
Mėnulis wedded the Sun and then courted the Morning Star; Perkūnas cut him with his sword, and so he wanes.

facets.facet_name: Virgin of the Air Whose Knee Bore the World
facets.core_claim: Ilmatar lay on the waters until the egg broke on her knee and became heaven and earth; with her hands she shaped the headlands and the deeps.
Tuoni's realm lies across the black river; whoever drinks Tuonetar's beer does not return.

facets.facet_name: King of the Waters and the Catch
facets.core_claim: Ahti rules the waters from his dwelling under the waves and gives fish to those who honour him.

facets.facet_name: King of the Forest and Its Game
facets.core_claim: Tapio holds the beasts of the forest; when the hunter sings well, he opens his golden storehouse.

facets.facet_name: The Hero Torn Apart and Restored by His Mother
facets.core_claim: Lemminkäinen was hewn to pieces in Tuoni's river; his mother gathered every piece and called him back to life.

facets.facet_name: Smith of the Sky-Vault and the Sampo
facets.core_claim: Ilmarinen forged the lid of heaven and the Sampo that grinds out grain, salt and gold.

facets.facet_name: Spirit of the Sacred Grove Turned Demon
facets.core_claim: Hiisi dwells in the dark woods and rocky hills; his creatures are the wasp, the snake and the disease-arrow.
Horagalles strikes the trolls with his hammers and guards people and reindeer from the powers that harm them.
Ráđđeáhčči is the highest; he creates the souls and sends them down, while his son does his work in the world.
facets.scholarly_note: Some scholars suspect Christian Trinitarian influence on the missionary-reported Radien family.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of Birth Under the Hearth
facets.core_claim: Sáráhkká forms the body of the child and opens the way at birth; she shares the mother's pain.
Juksáhkká holds the bow; she shapes the unborn and guards little children as they learn to walk.

facets.facet_name: Door Woman, Guardian of the Threshold
facets.core_claim: Uksáhkká dwells beneath the doorway and keeps watch over all who pass and over the child at birth.

facets.facet_name: Old Woman of the Realm of the Dead
facets.core_claim: Jábmeáhkká receives the dead below; the noaidi bargains with her for the souls of the sick.
Tharapita was born on the forest hill and flew to Ösel; there his people honoured him in the sacred grove.

facets.facet_name: The Old Heathen Outwitted by the Farmhand
facets.core_claim: Vanapagan owns great wealth and strength, but Kaval-Ants always tricks him out of it.

facets.facet_name: The Adversary Who Dove for the Earth
facets.core_claim: Ördög fetched the sand from which Isten made the earth, but kept some for himself, and so the world has rough mountains and his mischief.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Forest and Keeper of the First Arts
facets.core_claim: Basajaun protects the flocks and owned the wheat and the arts of the forge; humans won them by cunning.
Eguzki, grandmother sun, drives off the beings of the night and goes home to her mother the Earth at evening.
Armazi stands on the mountain above the royal city; the king and his people bow to him as lord of the land.

facets.facet_name: Patron of Men, Warriors and Travellers
facets.core_claim: Uastyrdzhi rides out to help travellers and warriors who call on him, and punishes the oath-breaker and the thief.

facets.facet_name: The Steel-Bodied Hero Who Fought Heaven
facets.core_claim: Batradz is the steel Nart; no blade can harm him, and he avenged his kin on the very spirits of heaven.

facets.facet_name: The Hero Whose Sword Is Returned to the Sea
facets.core_claim: Batradz would not die until his sword was cast into the sea; then the waters boiled and he could rest.
Uatsilla brings rain to the wheat and fire to the wrongdoer; one struck by his lightning is holy.

facets.facet_name: Ruler and Judge of the Dead
facets.core_claim: Barastyr sits at the entrance of the land of the dead and sends each soul to its place.
Kurdalægon's forge stands in heaven; he hardens heroes like steel and makes the arms of the Narts.
Thashxo is the creator who rules all; the other powers act by his will, and Habze is the way he has given.
Shible strikes with the lightning; whom he touches is his own, mourned with dancing rather than tears.
Tlepsh forged the tongs with his own hands and gave the Narts iron, the plough-share and the sickle.
Vahagn, born from the burning reed, wars against the vishaps and frees the waters and the land.

facets.facet_name: Straw-Thief Who Made the Milky Way
facets.core_claim: Vahagn carried off straw in winter, and the trail he scattered became the Straw-Thief's Way across the sky.

facets.facet_name: Little Star, Goddess of Love and Water
facets.core_claim: Astghik is the beloved of Vahagn; her festival scatters roses and water over the land.
Tir writes down what Aramazd decrees and reveals it to mortals in dreams.

facets.facet_name: The Earth and the World Beneath
facets.core_claim: Spandaramet is the earth that feeds the vine and receives the dead into its depths.
Perëndi is heaven above, who sends the thunder and to whom oaths are sworn.
facets.scholarly_note: The etymology (often *per- 'strike' + ndi 'sky/day', or from Latin imperator) is disputed.

facets.core_claim: Enji is the fire of the house; it is fed, respected and sworn by.
facets.scholarly_note: Reconstructed largely from the weekday name; a full cult is not documented.

facets.core_claim: The drangue rises into the storm to strike the kulshedra so that the rain may fall and the springs flow.
Kulshedra hoards the springs and burns the land; only the drangue's lightning can defeat her.
Lugus is the master of every skill and every road; the Gauls honour him above all and many images of him stand among them.
Esus cuts the sacred tree; offerings to him hang in the branches.
Belenus shines and heals; Aquileia trusted him to defend its walls.
Ogmios draws men after him by the chains of his speech; his strength is the word.
Rosmerta holds the cornucopia and the purse; with Mercury she brings plenty.
Taranis is the thunder; his wheel rolls across the sky, and Lucan names his altar as no less cruel than Scythian Diana's.
Teutates is the god of the people (teuta); the Berne scholiast says victims were drowned head-first in a vat for him.

facets.facet_name: The Spear-Struck God Restored from the Oak
facets.core_claim: Lleu could die only in an impossible place and way; slain, he became an eagle on the oak, and was sung back into his body.
With one cast he struck the wren between sinew and bone, and was named the Bright One of the Skilful Hand.
Brân's head kept company with his men in an otherworld feast and lay under the White Mount as the shield of the island.

facets.facet_name: Giant King and Giver of the Cauldron of Rebirth
facets.core_claim: Brân gave the cauldron that restores the dead to life, though they rise without speech.

facets.facet_name: The Divine Youth Stolen and Freed
facets.core_claim: Mabon was taken from between his mother and the wall; only the oldest of creatures knew where, and his release was the key to the great hunt.
Modron is the mother whose son was taken; through her the divine child returns.

facets.facet_name: Lady of the Silver Wheel Who Shapes Her Son's Destiny
facets.core_claim: Arianrhod, stepping over Math's wand, bore two sons; she swore fates upon Lleu that only Gwydion's cunning could undo.

facets.facet_name: Lady of the Hot Spring and Justice
facets.core_claim: Sulis heals in the steaming waters and avenges the wronged who write to her in lead.

facets.facet_name: Healer and Catcher at the Severn
facets.core_claim: Nodens heals those who sleep in his temple and recovers what is stolen.

facets.facet_name: The Sun Goddess, Healer and Charioteer
facets.core_claim: Sunna rides the sky and was called with the gods to charm Balder's horse whole again.
Tamfana's temple was the most famous among the tribes; to her the Marsi held their great feast.
In Baduhenna's grove the Frisians destroyed the invaders.

facets.facet_name: Typhon, the Monster Who Unmanned Zeus
facets.core_claim: Typhon, last child of Gaia and Tartarus, cut the sinews from Zeus's hands and feet and hid them in the Corycian cave, until Hermes stole them back and Zeus buried the monster under Etna.
Tyche turns the fortunes of every city and person; with the cornucopia and the rudder she gives and steers.

basis: Sumerian Nanna-Suen and Akkadian Sîn are the same moon god of Ur
Akkadian Sîn is the contracted form of Sumerian Suen
Same temple (Ekishnugal at Ur) and same family (son of Enlil, father of Shamash and Ishtar)
primary_text_evidence: Nabonidus inscriptions from Ur and Harran

basis: Both are young fertility gods who go down to the underworld
The land withers in their absence and revives on their return
Both are mourned by a goddess who seeks them
Both are youthful consorts of a great goddess
Both die and are ritually lamented
Their cult cycles mark seasonal death and renewal
Each must spend part of every year in the underworld
The division of the year below and above is a negotiated settlement
The arrangement explains the agricultural year
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Dumuzi and Geshtinanna alternate half-years; Persephone's share varies (one-third or half) in Greek sources.

basis: Both are kingly fertility gods who die and are mourned by a sister or wife
Both are tied to the vegetation cycle
Osiris remains below as king of the dead, while Dumuzi alternates
A deity withdraws in anger or grief and all fertility stops
Gods as well as humans begin to starve
Messengers search for and placate the deity
Return restores abundance
Absence of the god causes the failure of growth
Return of the god restores fertility
Telipinu departs in anger rather than dying
A deity departs in anger to a distant place
Gods are sent to find and soothe the deity
The return brings back moisture and fertility
Both are mediators between heaven, earth and the underworld
Both are represented with two entwined serpents on a staff
The Gudea libation vase is among the earliest images of the motif
parallels.scholarly_caveat: A direct line of transmission from Ningishzida's emblem to the Greek kerykeion is not demonstrated.

basis: Both are the primeval sea personified as a mother
Both give birth to the first generations of gods
Both precede the separation of heaven and earth
Both are the limitless primordial waters
All gods and the world emerge from them
Both remain as the encircling deep after creation
Both are the first undifferentiated state before the cosmos
From each, darkness and then light are generated
Nun is watery; Chaos is a gap or void
Ninurta's victory over Anzu and recovery of the Tablet of Destinies is the model for Marduk's victory over Tiamat and Kingu
Both are young champions summoned by the assembly when elder gods fail
Marduk absorbs Ninurta's epithets in Babylonian theology
parallels.scholarly_caveat: The derivation is widely argued from shared motifs; the exact literary dependence is debated.

basis: Sumerian Ishkur, Akkadian Adad and West Semitic Hadad are one storm god
All are written with the same logogram (dIM / dU)
Same functions: rain, thunder, the bull
Humanity is formed from the remains of punished divine rebels
Human nature therefore contains divine substance mixed with guilt
Kingu's blood / the Titans' soot after devouring Zagreus
Each holds supreme authority that is not rightfully his
Each is the creature of a rebellious mother-figure (Tiamat / Sophia)
Kingu is defeated and slain; Yaldabaoth remains world-ruler
Queen consort of the head of the pantheon
Shares in the decreeing of fates
Mother of major gods
Hittite Tarhunz and Hurrian Teshub are the same storm-king of the pantheon
Hittite scribes wrote both with the logogram dU
Both head the state pantheon beside a solar or celestial queen
parallels.source_tradition: Hittite state religion (Hurrianised under the New Kingdom)

basis: Both are the storm-kings of their pantheons, enthroned on Mount Hazzi / Zaphon
Ugaritic texts render Teshub as Baal in Hurrian–Ugaritic equivalence lists
Both defeat a sea or serpent power
Mount Zaphon of Baal is Mount Kasios, where Zeus Kasios was worshipped
Storm-king who wins kingship by defeating a chaos power
The Typhon battle is set at Mount Kasios in Greek sources
parallels.scholarly_caveat: Transmission from Levantine storm-god myth to Greek Zeus traditions is likely via Cilicia and Syria; extent debated.

basis: Storm-god who defeats a monstrous challenger to keep the kingship
Thunder is his weapon
Hurrian Kumarbi cycle and Hesiod's Theogony share the succession frame
Kumarbi bites off and swallows the genitals of the sky-god Anu; Kronos castrates Ouranos
Both are the middle generation of a three-step succession ending with the storm god
Both swallow a stone or their offspring
parallels.scholarly_caveat: The Hurrian-Hittite Kingship in Heaven cycle is widely held to be a source or close cousin of Hesiod's succession myth.

basis: Both are the sky-god castrated by his successor
Both are the first generation of the succession myth's line of kings
The Kumarbi cycle borrows the Mesopotamian Anu as its sky-king
An early king of heaven is deposed by a younger god
The deposed king goes down to the earth below
His reign belongs to the first age of the cosmos
A serpent-monster defeats the storm god and takes away his vital parts (heart and eyes / sinews)
The parts are recovered by trickery
The storm god then defeats the monster
Cosmic serpent overcome by the storm god
Victory over the serpent restores fertility
Celebrated in a seasonal festival (purulli)
Chaos power defeated by the storm god
Associated with waters
Victory confirms the storm god's kingship
A monster begotten by the deposed father-god (Kumarbi / Gaia's line) to overthrow the storm-king
It grows to threaten heaven itself
Both stories are located at Mount Hazzi / Kasios
Hittite scribes write Shaushka with the logogram IŠTAR
Shaushka of Nineveh is the Hurrian Ishtar of that city
Same union of love, war and boundary-crossing gender
Queen Puduhepa addresses the Sun Goddess of Arinna as the one whom in the land of cedars they call Hebat
Both are consort of the storm-king and queen of the state pantheon
Queen of heaven as consort of the storm-king
Mother of the divine heir
Leads the goddesses in procession/assembly
Female sun as the supreme deity of the state
She is the source of royal legitimacy
The ruler serves as her priest or descendant
Female ruler of the underworld
Hurrian Allani, Lelwani's counterpart, is equated with Ereshkigal
Receives offerings for the dead and for the ransom of the living
Divine king who judges souls in the underworld
Assisted by deities who weigh or present the dead
Also protector of the living kingship
City god who becomes the god of a state
Kings rule as his servants
Oaths and treaties sworn by him
Head of the pantheon associated with heaven
Protector of kingship
Elder high god above city patrons
Called mother of the gods
Great goddess paired with the head of the pantheon
Urartian Teisheba is the Hurrian Teshub under a Urartian name
Both are storm gods standing on a bull
Urartian and Hurrian are sister languages
Supreme national war god in whose might the king campaigns
Spoils of conquest dedicated to his temple
State pantheon structured around him
Sun god as one of the great gods of the state
Winged sun-disc iconography
All-seeing guarantor of order
Astarte (ʿAthtart) and Ishtar share the same Semitic name root ʿṯtr
Ugaritic equivalence lists match ʿAthtart with Ishtar
Both unite love, war and the Venus-star
parallels.scholarly_caveat: The goddesses are cognate and were syncretised, but their local cults remained distinct.

basis: Sumerian Inanna and Akkadian Ishtar are the same goddess in two languages
Bilingual hymns and god-lists equate them
Same myths (Descent) told in both languages
primary_text_evidence: Descent of Inanna / Descent of Ishtar

basis: Herodotus says the temple of Aphrodite Ourania at Ascalon is the oldest, and that the Cyprian and Cytheran cults came from it
Phoenician Astarte cult at Kition and Paphos on Cyprus, Aphrodite's island
Shared epithet Ourania / Queen of Heaven and the dove
